name: Rani of Jhansi
info: Lakshmibai, born Manikarnika Tambe, was queen consort of Jhansi from 1843 to 1853 and took over its rule in 1857, fighting the British in the Indian Rebellion until she died in battle at Gwalior in 1858.

facts.born: Varanasi, as Manikarnika Tambe, called Manu; daughter of Moropant Tambe, a Karhada Brahmin in the service of the Maratha noble Chimaji, and Bhagirathi. Her birth year is disputed: 1827 in British sources, 1835 in most Indian sources, between 1828 and 1830 for the historians Tapti Roy and Rudrangshu Mukherjee
facts.died: 18 June 1858, in battle against British forces near Gwalior; the exact manner of her death is unknown, but all accounts agree she died fighting
facts.role: Queen consort of the princely state of Jhansi from 1843 to 1853; leader of Jhansi from June 1857 until the British captured it in April 1858; one of the leading figures of the Indian Rebellion of 1857
facts.known: her appeals against the annexation of Jhansi under the doctrine of lapse; her rule of Jhansi in 1857 to 1858; the Siege of Jhansi and her escape from the fort; the last stand at Gwalior; the contested question of her part in the killing of the British at Jhansi; her place in Indian nationalism

t: Married as a child to the raja of Jhansi, Lakshmibai lost her infant son and then her husband, and the East India Company annexed Jhansi in 1854 under the doctrine of lapse in spite of her appeals.
After sepoys mutinied at Jhansi in June 1857 and nearly all the British there were killed, she took over its rule; whether she took part in the killings was and remains contested.
Hugh Rose captured Jhansi in April 1858, and she died fighting at Gwalior that June; she became a heroine of Indian nationalism, a reading that Dalit writers dispute.
dyk: In 1943 Subhas Chandra Bose, recognising the Rani's symbolism, called for female volunteers for the Indian National Army, who were formed into the Rani of Jhansi Regiment and trained in Singapore.
ev: Manikarnika Tambe is born in Varanasi, a date placed between 1828 and 1830 by Roy and Mukherjee but given as 1827 or 1835 in other sources
According to Indian sources, she marries the raja of Jhansi, Gangadhar Rao, in May and becomes the Rani Lakshmibai
She gives birth to a son, who dies at a few months old
Gangadhar Rao adopts Damodar Rao and dies on 21 November
The Company rejects her appeals, and Jhansi lapses to it in May
Sepoys mutiny at Jhansi in June, most of the British are killed on 8 June, and she proclaims her rule on the sepoys' departure
Hugh Rose besieges Jhansi from 22 March; the town falls on 3 April and she escapes from the fort that night
She dies in battle near Gwalior on 18 June, and Rose captures the city the next day

sections.early:
Little is known for certain about Lakshmibai's life before 1857, and every biography of her relies on a mixture of factual evidence and legendary tales, especially for her childhood and adolescence. She was born Manikarnika Tambe in Varanasi, the daughter of Moropant Tambe, a Karhada Brahmin who served the Maratha noble Chimaji, and his wife Bhagirathi. Manikarnika was an epithet of the River Ganges, and in childhood she was known as Manu. Her birth year is disputed. British sources tended towards 1827 and Indian sources generally preferred 1835, but the historians Tapti Roy and Rudrangshu Mukherjee have argued that the later date is implausible because of chronological irregularities, and place her birth between 1828 and 1830.

Her mother died when she was four, a year after the death of Chimaji. Moropant then moved to the court of Baji Rao at Bithur, who had been deposed as Maratha peshwa in 1817; Baji Rao gave him a job and became fond of the girl. According to uncorroborated popular legend, her playmates at Bithur included Nana Sahib and Tatya Tope, who would also become prominent in 1857. The stories say that she was allowed to play and learn with them, that she was literate and skilled in horseriding, and that she was given lessons in fencing, swordplay and even firearms, which would have been extremely unusual for a girl.
sections.rise:
It is presumed that Baji Rao brought Manikarnika to the attention of Gangadhar Rao, the old raja of Jhansi, who had no children and greatly desired an heir. Moropant accepted the marriage offer, and according to Indian sources the couple wed in May 1842. On that chronology she was seven years old and the marriage was not consummated until she was fourteen. She was given the name Lakshmi, after the Hindu goddess, and was thereafter the Rani Lakshmibai. Both British and Indian sources portray Gangadhar Rao as uninterested in rulership, but British sources call him debauched and imbecilic while Indian sources read the same traits as signs of a cultured nature. According to popular legend he turned a blind eye to her equipping and training of an armed all-female regiment, though if it existed it was probably formed after his death.

In 1851 she gave birth to a son amid much rejoicing, but he died at a few months old. As the raja's health failed, he adopted on his deathbed a five-year-old relative, Anand Rao, renamed Damodar Rao, and died on 21 November 1853. Two days before, he had written to Company officials asking them to recognise Damodar Rao as ruler and Lakshmibai as his regent. Jhansi had been ceded to the East India Company in 1817, and the Company had for several years enforced a doctrine of lapse, annexing states whose Hindu rulers died without a natural heir.
sections.deeds:
Lakshmibai wrote on 16 February 1854 to protest against the annexation, and Governor-General Lord Dalhousie answered eleven days later. He described Gangadhar Rao's rule as one of decline and mismanagement, said that Jhansi would benefit from direct British rule, and argued that since the British had conquered the Marathas, Jhansi's former overlords, the Company was the paramount power with authority over the succession. She pursued the case through diplomatic channels, talking with a sympathetic Company official, Major Ellis, and engaging the Australian lawyer John Lang. Her appeals cited treaties of 1803, 1817 and 1842 that recognised the rajas of Jhansi, and Hindu shastra tradition on adoption. Dalhousie rejected them without refuting their arguments, and Jhansi lapsed to the Company in May 1854. She received a lifetime pension of five thousand rupees per month (or £6,000 yearly) and had to leave the fort but kept the palace. The Company held her liable for 36,000 rupees of her husband's debt, an issue never resolved.

After the sepoys left Jhansi on 11 June 1857, she officially proclaimed that she had assumed its rulership. Major Erskine, commissioner of the Saugor division, authorised her to rule until the British returned. She collected taxes, repaired the fort and distributed donations to the poor. Her general Jawahar Singh defeated Sadasheo Rao, who twice tried to claim Jhansi, and Jhansi repelled Orchha and Datia, which invaded on 10 August and besieged it until late October, when the raja of Banpur's troops drove them off. She then ordered the recruitment of troops and the manufacture of cannon.
sections.opponents:
On 5 June 1857 sepoys at Jhansi took the ammunition store and shot their British commanding officer, and the remaining sixty British men, women and children took refuge in the fort. On 8 June they surrendered and asked for safe passage; they were led to the Jokhan Bagh garden, where nearly all of them were killed. The Rani's part in the killings is debated. S. Thornton, a tax collector, wrote that she had instigated the revolt, and two somewhat questionable eyewitness accounts said that she executed three British messengers and falsely promised the rest safe passage. Other contemporary reports held her innocent, and the official report by F.W. Pinkney came to no clear conclusion. In two mid-June letters to Erskine she said that she had been at the mercy of the mutineers. Erskine believed her, but his superiors were less trusting; items belonging to the dead were later found in her palace, and Roy has pointed to the active part of her father Moropant. She had supplied the sepoys with a thousand men and two guns after they threatened her palace and her life.

The British probably decided she was an enemy because of her conflict with Orchha and the rebels' presence in Jhansi, and religious anti-British pamphlets wrongly attributed to her reached British intelligence. Charles Canning later declared her a rebel leader and set a bounty of 20,000 rupees on her. Indian narratives have struggled most with the massacre: either she took part from the outset and so stained her virtue, or she was a reluctant participant, which makes her later heroism less intentional than the nationalist account demands.
sections.last:
Major General Hugh Rose, commanding the Central India Field Force, reached Jhansi in March 1858. By then the Rani was still sending conciliations to the British while preparing arms, and some advisers urged peace, others, including her father, war. Her troops may have decided the matter by demanding to fight. The siege began on 22 March with artillery fire, and Tatya Tope's relief army of more than 20,000 was defeated at the Battle of Betwa on 1 April. British columns entered the town at 3 am on 3 April. The Rani led a counter-attack with 1,500 Afghan troops but was driven back, and the British killed around three thousand people. Her father Moropant escaped, was captured and was executed on 20 April. She left the fort that night with about three hundred soldiers, her adopted son tied to her waist; accounts of how she escaped differ and the British one told by Lyster is questionable.

She reached Kalpi at midnight on 5 April. The rebel army there passed her over for command in favour of Tatya Tope, and after Rose's victories at Kunch and Kalpi, where her advice was ignored, the rebels moved to Gwalior Fort. On 17 June Rose attacked. At about 7:30 am the Eighth Hussars scattered her bodyguard, and an eyewitness said she charged them. The manner of her death is unknown. She died on 18 June 1858, probably cremated by her followers, and Rose took Gwalior the next day. Damodar Rao lost the 600,000 rupees held for him and received a pension of 150 rupees a month.
sections.legacy:
Rose wrote that she was "remarkable for her beauty, cleverness, perseverance [and] generosity to her subordinates" and, in his battle report, the "best and bravest of the rebels"; one British officer felt that the "beast of Jhansi" had too easy a death. Her story became closely tied to Indian nationalism. Naming her in literature symbolised a nationalist spirit the British-controlled state media prohibited, and the independence movement saw her as a hero in the mould of Shivaji. In 1943 Subhas Chandra Bose formed the Rani of Jhansi Regiment of women volunteers, who served in support roles in Burma and never fought in combat. Oral tradition linked her to Durga, Lakshmi and Shakti, and the Indian National Congress and Hindutva proponents have each claimed her for their own aims.

Dalit communities tend to view her negatively. Dalit writers have promoted heroes such as Jhalkaribai, whose accounts often present her as the Rani's equal or superior and sometimes call the Rani a coward, and festivals for the two women are attended by different communities. The best-known literary works are Subhadra Kumari Chauhan's 1930 poem "Jhansi Ki Rani" and Vrindavan Lal Verma's 1946 novel, which invented the quotation "I will never give up my Jhansi!" often attributed to her. No contemporary portrait of her survives.

summary: Lakshmibai (born Manikarnika Tambe between 1827 and 1835, died 1858) was queen of Jhansi, which the Company annexed in 1854 despite her appeals. She ruled it in 1857, her part in the killing of the British there remains contested, and she died fighting at Gwalior in 1858.
references: Joyce Lebra, The Rani of Jhansi: A Study in Female Heroism in India (University of Hawai'i Press, 1986)
Rudrangshu Mukherjee, A Begum and a Rani: Hazrat Mahal and Lakshmibai in 1857 (Penguin Random House India, 2021)
Tapti Roy, Raj of the Rani (Penguin Books, 2006)
Harleen Singh, The Rani of Jhansi: Gender, History, and Fable in India (Cambridge University Press, 2014)
notes: Birth year: lede '1827-30, or 1835'; body says British sources 1827, Indian sources 1835, Roy and Mukherjee 1828-1830. start 1828 with circa true; the facts line gives all versions. Event 'c. 1828' stated with the spread.
Marriage in May 1842 is 'according to Indian sources' (traditional chronology); the lede says she was queen consort from 1843 to 1853. Event dated 1842 with attribution.

Gwalior/Kotah-ki-Serai: the article gives the battle date as 17 June attack and the lede gives death on 18 June 1858; the article's body does not state the date of the Hussars' charge. I give 17 June for Rose's attack and 18 June for her death as the lede does; the editor should check that 'at about 7:30 am' falls on 18 June (the body places it after the attack ordered on the 17th).
Escape: the article gives several accounts; only the Lyster one is named (called questionable by the article). The horse-jump and lowering accounts left out.
The article says she arrived at Kalpi at midnight on 5 April (more reliable sources); legends of one night's ride of 102 miles left out. Cremation is 'likely' per the article.
The 'Eighth Hussars' charge and 'Mundar' companion: companion left out as 'possibly'.

The 15,000/125,000 rupee ransom to sepoys left out for space. The Rani 'provided a thousand men and two guns' is the article's account per a servant of a British captain; I give it as part of the sepoys' threat, which the article reports only through that servant: the editor may want it attributed.
Moropant's execution date 20 April given; the article says 'Moropant was captured and, on 20 April, executed'.
Left out as uncorroborated: friendship with Nana Sahib and Tatya Tope beyond the legend; the all-female regiment (hedged); 'I will never give up my Jhansi' (only as invented for the 1946 novel).
Literature section: British portrayals (Kali, Joan of Arc, Flashman) and films left out as the guide excludes films and fiction about the person.
'Dalit communities tend to view her negatively' is the lede's wording; the Jhalkaribai accounts are described as Dalit accounts, not as fact.
